evidence.note: Up front catalogued slot limits (valu=6, load=2, etc.), VLEN=8, 32 vectors/batch, and derived that <1250 requires ~16 batch elements/cycle — quantitative floor reasoning before any optimization.
Computed load floor (4096/2=2048) and valu floor (12288/6=2048), identified both engines saturated at the 2048 bound, and set numeric targets (loads→~2500, valu→~7500) to close the gap to 1250.

Recomputed per-engine floors as ops changed (valu 1549, load 1417, flow 770), identified valu as bottleneck, and quantified the ~665-cycle gap to measured as scheduling/dep-chain overhead to prioritize next steps.

Tracked floors shifting to load-bound (1669) then balanced (1416/1416), used 'measured − floor = 605' to decide whether to reduce op counts vs improve scheduling, and drove specialization level (k) choices by their measured cycle effect.
Computed the hash critical-path dependency chain (17 deps × 16 rounds = 272 cycles) to rule out critical path as the binding constraint — SIMD-width + dependency modeling.

Derived the hard load-bound wall (12 general rounds × 256 / 2 = 1536), concluded the kernel is near-optimal for this algorithm, and identified that only reducing gather count could reach <1250 — recognizing near-floor state.

reasoning: The agent constructed explicit cost models tying instruction counts and slot occupancy to cycles, continuously estimated per-engine theoretical floors, and used the measured-vs-floor gap to choose which engine to attack and which transforms to try (level 8 fully met). It further derived floors from slot limits, SIMD width, and a critical-path dependency chain, used them to reject non-productive transforms and to recognize when the kernel was near-optimal and why <1250 was unreachable without a different algorithm (level 10 behavior). I hold it at 9 rather than 10 because a large persistent floor-to-measured gap was never rigorously modeled, only attributed vaguely to scheduler/dependency overhead.
